Industry News: Best Cutting Boards for Slicing, Dicing, and Chopping (2026)

📅 11 Nov 2020 | ⏱️ 33 min read (6652 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~33 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A good cutting board is an essential kitchen tool that provides a layer of protection between your knife and your countertop.
  • New in this patch: After much consideration and years of testing different boards, we decided to shift our top recommendations for wood boards to feature only end-grain options.
  • Sources indicate that A butcher block board from Texas’s Boardsmith won’t come cheap, but we think a large and sturdy wood cutting board is a worthy kitchen investment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A good cutting board is an essential kitchen tool that provides a layer of protection between your knife and your countertop. But the best cutting boards do more than just protect your counters during food prep—they provide a stable surface when you’re vigorously chopping and act as a protective surface that prevents prematurely dulling the blades of your kitchen knives. Cutting boards come in a variety of materials: plastic, wood, rubber, even glass and metal for inexplicable reasons. After testing dozens of boards of all sorts of materials over the course of six years, we have found five favorites. Read on to find out which might be best for you as well as how we tested and what we look for in the cutting boards we want to use every day.

New in this patch: After much consideration and years of testing different boards, we decided to shift our top recommendations for wood boards to feature only end-grain options. They’re easier on knives and more beautiful to keep on the counter. And our new top pick is reasonably priced as end-grain boards go. For more on what makes end- and edge-grain boards different, click here. And if you’re looking for a quality (but truly inexpensive) wood board, we’d encourage you to look at these two Boos boards. They’re edge-grain, so they’ll wear your knives more swiftly, but Boos makes almost universally great cutting boards.

Maple End-Grain Cutting Board (18" x 12").

Sources indicate that A butcher block board from Texas’s Boardsmith won’t come cheap, but we think a large and sturdy wood cutting board is a worthy kitchen investment. A good wood cutting board can last decades and decades, and since it will likely live permanently on your counter, function as a key aesthetic component of your kitchen. Our editors have used this heavy-duty piece for over a year in their home kitchens, and even after daily use, it indicates little to no wear and only minimal staining.

Sources indicate that what we love: The craftsmanship on the board is apparent as soon as you take it out of the box. The offset pattern of the individual pieces of wood is striking (as it is on most end-grain boards). And its construction feels smooth and solid.

As an end-grain board, it’s easy on knife blades, leaving them sharper than a less expensive edge-grain board. The real highlights, beyond the pure aesthetics, are in the small design features, though. Senior shopping editor Noah Kaufman has been using it in his home kitchen since June of 2025 and has found it the most stable board he’s ever used. That’s thanks to the addition of four grippy silicone-tipped feet on one side (you can order a Boardsmith without the feet, but you’d be giving away that stability). Those feet also raise the board up a little higher on the counter—which prevents the underside from retaining moisture and warping—and for Noah, they elevate the board to a very comfortable cutting height. It’s also reversible, with an effective, though not too deep, juice groove on the side of the footed side.

Boardsmith’s end-grain boards are very customizable. They come in four sizes (we tested the 18" x 12" x 2", but the largest—24" x 18" x 2"—would make a beautiful always-out piece), three wood types (in addition to the maple, we tried walnut and cherry), and you can opt for features like juice and finger grooves. The feet are also optional, though they’re included by default, so you have to check a box if you want a board without feet.

What we’d leave: Again, this board is heavy, which makes it sturdy, but also a bit of a chore to clean. Because it’s wood, it also requires some upkeep in the form of oiling and buttering (the brand’s Board Butter has kept the surface of the Noah’s board in tip-top shape through months of use). Finally, while the feet are a vital feature, they do make the board a little less attractive if left on the counter with the juice groove facing up. But using the groove is a less frequent use than regular slicing and chopping, so you’ll be more likely to leave it feet side down—or at least turn it back over after you’re done cutting and cleaning.

It has been revealed that in the long run: With long-term testing of a full year, the Boardsmith has stood up in a way that justifies its high price. It’s held on to minimal stains, and with a bit of oil and wax every three to four weeks, the board looks as beautiful as it did when it arrived.

R-Board Series Rectangular Wooden Maple Cutting Board, 18”x12”.

Boos boards, as they’re commonly called, are pretty much the gold standard for wood cutting boards, and this relatively affordable maple cutting board is a dream to cut on.

What we love: Though maple is a hard wood, the cutting surface is smooth and has the perfect amount of give. In our testing, it seemed to almost embrace the knife blade with each chop. The board didn’t retain any food odors and it was easy to hand-wash (never put a wood board in the dishwasher!). Even beet juice disappeared after a good cleaning.

Boos Blocks come in many different sizes, we’ve found that the 18x12" size is just right for most home kitchens. This board is from the brand’s R-Board series, and it’s substantial without being too massive. There’s plenty of room to carve a roast chicken, but it’s small enough to slide into the cabinet where you keep your sheet pans (a half-sheet is 18x13") as long as you don’t have too much else in there. At 2.25" it’s the tallest (thickest) cutting board we tested, and it will add significant height to your cooking zone, which is something shorter home cooks should always keep in mind when choosing a chopping board.

Industry observers note that what we’d leave: Though not necessarily a negative, this board is on the heavy side (10 lb.), and it does require frequent oiling to keep it in tip-top shape. Boos recommends their proprietary Mystery Oil and Board Cream, and if you buy directly from the brand, you can bundle the care products with the board.

What we love: Sonder’s board is beautiful, and like the Boardsmith, it features end-grain construction, which is easier on knives because they slide between the wood fibers, avoiding friction with the hard surface. End-grain boards also “self-heal,” which means that the fibers come back together after having been sliced—and I found that after rigorous use in a week of endless chopping tests, this board came out looking as beautiful as it had when it came out of the package. This board is made of American walnut and constructed in the US.

The Sonder board also has some clever design elements: It’s hard to find an end-grain board that features a juice groove at this price point (the Boardsmith below, for example, costs almost $100 more). Flip the board over, and on the other side, it features three carved-out compartments, so you can slide chopped food to the side as you prep, keeping ingredients contained, separated, and out of the way. Those compartments can also be used for a fun charcuterie board setup: Use them to hold sauces and condiments or as a landing place for olive pits. Both sides of the board feature grippy rubber feet, and I found that this board stayed steady and level on the countertop even during heavy-duty chopping.

This board was less cumbersome to take to the sink and hand wash than many of the large end-grain boards we tried. It has ergonomic handles carved into the sides, which makes for easy transport despite its heft and size. And because it’s a dark-colored wood, it shows less sign of staining than other wooden boards.

In a recent development, what we’d leave: There’s not much fault to find in Sonder’s board beyond the standard caveats that an end-grain cutting board requires maintenance in the form of regular oiling and must be hand-washed. The prep grooves are a nice feature, but they aren’t as useful if you’re used to using a bench scraper, since it can’t fit in them. At $179, the Sonder is a bit pricey, but the benefits of end-grain over a cheaper edge-grain board are worth the bump up. If you’re concerned about price primarily, you should opt for the plastic Oxo board recommended below. Because of the carved-in prep containers on one side of the board, you have limited chopping space (but you always have the option to use the other side, which offers a full surface).

What we love: Senior reviews editor, Olivia Tarantino, owns three types of cutting boards (wood, composite, and the MK Midi), and the Midi is the one she grabs for anything short of a full dinner. “It’s closer to midsize than small, which makes it more versatile than a mini board that’s only good for smashing garlic. I can dice a whole onion, slice a tomato, and even fit a mise en place of scallion, ginger, and garlic. Because it’s nonporous, it’s my pick over wood for wetter ingredients, since I can toss it in the dishwasher when I’m done,” she indicates, noting that she owns the white color and there’s no staining after eight months. The one downside worth noting is that the surface is a bit harder, which can be tougher on knives.

Adding a smaller board like this to a kitchen that already has a large wood cutting board can help for small prep work like slicing fruit, vegetables, or ingredients like garlic without having to clean your big board in between.

What we’d leave: We wish that Material would add feet to the larger version of the board. If it’s all you’ve got, a small cutting board can be frustratingly limiting. Also, after years of working with Material’s cutting boards in their homes, our editors noted that they will show visible wear and tear in the form of slice marks and small stains. This is inevitable for any plastic (or similar) cutting board.

Good Grips Plastic Utility Cutting Board.

According to recent reports, what we love: This plastic cutting board from Oxo is very popular in the BA Test Kitchen. It’s budget-friendly and dishwasher-safe and comes with a juice groove. At 14.75" x 10.4", it’s a good size for meal prep, the plastic cutting surface is nonporous, and silicone strips run the length of both short sides to help keep it in place on the counter when cutting. It’s also reversible with one side offering a channel to catch meat juices.

What we'd leave: The Oxo isn’t very attractive, so you wouldn’t want to use it as a serving board. Also, the longevity of a plastic board like this is only a couple of years, and if you chop too rigorously, the board has been known to shed plastic particles. If you are concerned about plastic use in the kitchen, this isn’t your board.

Yoshihiro Hi-Soft High Performance Professional Grade Cutting Board.

Rubber cutting boards are seen more often in professional kitchens than home ones, but if you’re looking for something large and durable, and you don’t want to have to bust out your knife sharpener regularly, consider this Hi-Soft rubber board by Yoshihiro. It’s very knife-friendly, and cutting on it feels nice. It stays in place on the counter, and unlike another rubber board we tested, it doesn’t have a rubber tire odor.

It has been revealed that what we love: There are a couple of reasons chefs like food-safe rubber cutting surfaces. For starters, because rubber has a little give, the cutting surface flexes ever so slightly to the knife edge versus wearing it down like a hard surface would. Both synthetic and natural rubber are also nonporous, so they’re easier to sanitize than wood boards and are often used by sushi chefs for that reason (conversely, wood cutting boards are actually health-code violations in some cities).

According to recent reports, what we'd leave: Though sanitizing the surface is easy, large rubber boards can be harder to wash because, in addition to being significant, they are also heavier than, say, plastic, and the rubber material must be washed by hand. Rubber cutting boards can also hold on to stains more easily than plastic.

In the long run: With its light color this board has shown a bit of staining and evidence of knife blades running across it. But all things considered, it’s cleaned up very well and proven an excellent companion to an always-out end-grain wood board.

Before getting the knives out, we researched chopping boards and narrowed down a selection that included a wide range of plastic, rubber, and various types of wood boards that ranged from about $10 to almost $300.

To assess the boards’ durability and stability, testers chopped a pound of carrots, diced a large onion, and minced fresh ginger. Testers also cut steamed beets on each board so they could see how much (or how little) each board held on to stains. We chopped lots of garlic on the boards and watched out over the course of the days and weeks of testing for odor retention on the boards. Finally, we washed each board according to the directions and oiled the wood boards that called for it.

Here is an example of the kind of staining you can expect with a wood cutting board. A good scrub with some coarse salt and lemon juice will help take care of this.

These are the qualities we looked for in the best cutting boards.

We recommend that home kitchens have one large cutting board, ideally around 20" x 15". Additionally, it’s useful to have some supplemental smaller plastic or wood cutting boards (in the 16" x 12" and 12" x 8" ranges) that are easier to transport to the sink for washing or that fit in the dishwasher. You’ll have your bases covered when you have a large board that can take on any large cooking prep task without risk of vegetables flying all over the kitchen, or upon which you can plop a giant piece of meat for carving—but also some small boards that can be used daily for lighter prep, eliminating the need for a daily full-scale clean of your large board.

During testing, I also looked out for board height; if your board is too tall, it adds too much height to the counter, making it awkward for shorter home cooks to get a good angle when cutting. A too big or too heavy board is also hard to clean and move.

We recommend rubber, wood, and plastic cutting boards. There’s a trade-off involved in selecting the right hardness level for a cutting board. A material that’s too hard will have you busting out your knife sharpener more often than you should, while a board that’s too soft will end up with cut marks so deep you may no longer have a smooth surface—and it will be harder to clean and sanitize. So you want a durable surface that will feel nice to cut on and have some give. For wood cutting boards, we prioritized boards made with American materials. That’s particularly important because wood sourced abroad is often less sustainably sourced, first because it needs to be shipped overseas, and second because the US has more rigorous forestry regulations than some other countries. For a pro-and-con comparison of the various cutting board materials, scroll farther down the page.

Recent findings suggest that if the board had a special feature, like grippers or a juice channel, we evaluated how functional the features actually were. We measured the amount of liquid the juice grooves held and used any prep compartments.

Chop-N-Slice Series Rectangular Wood Maple Cutting Board, 18" x 12".

If you have your heart set on a Boos Board but don’t have a lot of space or want to spend a lot of money, this reversible board from the John Boos Chop-N-Slice series is a high-quality board with a pretty low price tag. It’s made of durable maple wood and arrives oiled (it only barely held on to stains from steamed beets). It’s only 1.25" thick, which contributes to its low price. Though it’s not too big or heavy, it has handle grooves on both ends, which can be helpful if you’re carrying a loaded board. Right out of the box, we felt the board was a little rough, but with a touch of seasoning, it significantly improved.

Rectangular Wood Maple Cutting Board.

This end-grain cutting board was a joy to chop on thanks to its soft and responsive surface—it genuinely felt the best of any of the wood boards we tested. Chopping feels ergonomic and your knife feels protected. The board is also beautiful and would stand proudly in a permanent place on anyone’s kitchen counter. When it arrived, it felt dry and chalky, so it immediately needed to be oiled and treated, whereas the winning end-grain boards felt more ready to go out of the box. And unlike the Boardsmith and Sonder boards, it doesn’t have a juice groove.

It also seemed slightly uneven or warped from the beginning: The board wobbled back and forth ever so slightly during rigorous chopping, making a slight clanking noise. This was almost imperceptible, and since we’ve used Boos boards over the years and loved their stability and durability, we think it’s likely the flaw of the particular board we tested. So we’d still absolutely recommend Boos end-grain boards.

Large End Grain Prep Station Acacia Wood Cutting Board.

This inexpensive end-grain board comes highly recommended by other review sites, and at $72 at the time of writing, it’s an excellent value for an acacia wood board. Its dark color makes it resistant to showing stains, and after being put through its chopping paces, it had no scratches. However, the board did arrive with a visible scratched-up patch on its lower right corner. Even though it was an end-grain board, I didn’t find it as soft or responsive as the Boos above or either of our winning boards. And the wood isn’t sourced domestically. Still, this is a solid value option.

Sources indicate that if you’re looking for a large and inexpensive board, this 20" x 15" option from TeakHaus is a good choice. The high-quality edge-grain teak looks great, and the darker wood won’t show stains like lighter-colored wood boards do. Cutting felt comfortable, and one side of this reversible board features a juice groove. It’s an inch-and-a-half tall, and that combined with the size makes it pretty bulky. Also, the smell of ginger lingered on this one a bit after we hand-washed it.

This Kickstarter-funded design isn’t just a cutting board; it’s a whole modular prep station. The cutting board has magnetic sides, onto which snap carved wood prep bowls fitted with stainless-steel containers (or silicone liners, depending on which package you opt for). Those bowls also stack nicely on top of the board for storage, and everything can be arranged and rearranged at the cook’s convenience.

It has been revealed that the design here is clever: It’s satisfying to move the board and containers around because everything fits together in a delightful little puzzle, and attaching the prep bowls produces a satisfying click. The magnetic connection is very secure, and it’s helpful and convenient to have little prep bowls available for sweeping away items as you chop them.

According to recent reports, you can select various attachable container sizes, and there’s even a large one that runs the whole length of the cutting board that can be used to set up a dredging station for chicken cutlets. You can also buy lids that fit the containers so that they can go right in the fridge to store leftover prepped items, or sauces you made ahead of time for a dinner party.

It has been revealed that we like a lot of what’s going on here, but the board’s edge-grain maple construction doesn’t feel high-quality—it was chalky and rough upon arrival. The system is available in a variety of wood types, so maybe the walnut or Brazilian teak that we didn’t test would fare better. But the system is pricey ($519 for a 13-piece set), and the space you’re offered on the actual cutting surface is limited, so there’s not a ton of room for actual chopping—you dedicate a lot of the counter real estate to the attachable containers. If you’ve been in the market for nice prep containers just as much as you have been for a cutting board and love the idea of a smartly designed holistic system, you’ll like the Chef Station. We love the design in theory, but on the merits of the cutting board alone, it’s not a test winner.

Maple Wood Kitchen Basic Cutting Board.

In a recent development, the JK Adams Maple Wood Basic Cutting Board is made of durable maple. It has a minimal design with no embellishments and won’t add too much height to your prep zone. At just ¾" thick, it’s the thinnest wood board tested. The 17" x 14" footprint also offers a decent amount of space for cutting and chopping but is compact enough to keep in a small kitchen.

In a recent development, the JK Adams Pour Spout Cutting Board stands out because it has a juice groove and a pouring spout on both sides, making it truly reversible for cutting meat. Though this is a sizable board at 20" x 14", the groove and spout do take up a significant portion of the surface area available for cutting, so keep that in mind if you’re looking for something to use for really large cuts of meat. The wood is light-colored and will show stains from something like beets, but keeping it treated with beeswax and mineral oil will provide some stain resistance.

Material Kitchen’s MK Free Board is made entirely of plant-based materials ("100% plant-based biocomposite of natural clay minerals and biodegradable biopolymers," according to Material’s website). That last part is important—especially if you're concerned about microplastics—because this board has none, hence the name. It's dishwasher-safe and has a loop that makes it easy to pull out of a cabinet or hang from a hook. Overall, it’s a totally fine cutting board you can feel very good about using, but without some plant-based bumpers on the bottom, it won’t get a top spot in our rankings. While the microplastic-free material is wonderful in theory, it feels a bit harder on your knives, and because it doesn't have silicone corners, it’s more prone to sliding around on a quartz countertop. And without anything to soften its landing, the thinner, harder material is also fairly loud.

Silicone Cutting Boards Mats, Set of 3.

If you’re looking for a nonporous alternative to plastic, rubber is our first pick. But both natural and synthetic rubber cutting boards are pricey, so you might want to consider a silicone cutting board. It’s vital to note that these are mats, not actual boards. But even at ⅛" thick, the material provided a reasonable barrier between the knife and counter. Silicone is flexible so it’s easy to fold into a U-shape to transfer ingredients to a pot or scraps to the trash. These mats are also dishwasher-safe even though they’re very easy to hand-wash. And since the entire mat is silicone, it’s very nonslip. These also have built-in grooves around the entire perimeter and a hole in the corner for hanging and so far, they haven’t held on to any stains (even from steamed beets) or shown any knife marks (even when we tried to make some). That said, some customers on Amazon have reported knife damage to their mats, which could be a result of the silicone degrading. Though silicone is durable and heat tolerant, repeated exposure to high heat or sudden temperature changes can weaken its structural integrity, and it can hold on to stains.

Sources indicate that the All Aboard cutting board from colorful cookware brand Great Jones is like the original Material reBoard’s bigger, curvier cousin. At 16" x 12", it’s substantial for a plastic board, and it has a nice loop/handle for hanging. It’s made of BPA-free recycled plastic, and the textured surface is nice to cut on. It doesn't have any sort of silicone grip to keep it in place on the counter when cutting, but it does have a juice groove.

Sources indicate that these double-sided boards come in three sizes; one side has a juice groove and the other has an indentation along the top intended to hold Caraway’s tiny Dot & Dash containers. The boards are made from eco-friendly birch, which is lightweight compared to other woods but feels more like maple when cutting. These boards are also pretty thin, so I have concerns about warping, though limiting exposure to moisture can help with that. The board also comes oiled, though it did hold on to some strawberry and beet stains—as we’d expect any wood board to do.

Architec Original Gripper Cutting Board.

Sources indicate that this 14" x 11" polypropylene (plastic) cutting board is fine but nothing special. It comes in a variety of fun colors, it has a handle hole you can use to hang it, and it’s dishwasher-safe. One side has small rubber feet (a.k.a. the “nonslip gripper” base), which does keep the board stationary but also makes it so you can only use one side for chopping.

Epicurean Kitchen Series Cutting Board.

In a recent development, as much as we love Epicurean’s multipurpose cooking utensil, the brand’s cutting board is a no-go. There’s much to like; the nonporous wood composite is dishwasher-safe and won’t warp or splinter like wood. Plus, it looks so much nicer than plastic. But one reason it’s so durable is that it’s so hard, which made everyone who tried it worry about their knife blades. It was also very loud to use. The pricier nonslip version (which also has a juice groove) was slightly more pleasant to use, but still not recommended.

At 14.9" x 19.6", this versatile bamboo carving board from Meater (the wireless thermometer brand) offers great surface area. One side is solid and free from embellishments, while the other features a sizable juice groove and pouring spout. But the light-colored wood stained fairly easily in testing and required intense scrubbing after we cut beets on it. And we no longer recommend bamboo cutting boards because the surface is extremely hard on knife edges.

Steelport Steelcore Cutting Board.

The Steelport Steelcore cutting board is a thin, sexy board from the maker of the also sexy Steelport knives. It’s a dual-sided board; one side is thin, perfectly smooth end-grain walnut, and the other is a durable recycled paper composite material. Embedded between the two is a steel core to prevent the board from warping. The surfaces are incredibly smooth, and the composite side has a juice groove, which maintains the modern look of the end-grain side. Unfortunately, the board we received had hairline cracks which, without the steel core, would have probably knocked three corners off of this board. For such a pricey piece of gear, it wasn’t well-packaged for cross-country transit. But the fact that the board stayed fully intact even with three cracked corners is a testament to the strength of the steel core.

In a recent development, made In’s tableware, cookware, and kitchen tools have a lot of fans at BA, and I wanted to love Made In’s edge-grain Butcher Block. One side is a solid butcher block surface without any grooves or embellishments, while the other features a juice groove. At 17.75" x 11.75", it’s also a nice size for big cuts of meat or to use as a charcuterie board. Unfortunately, even though it’s “steamed for durability” and appeared to come oiled out of the box, the surface really indicated marks from the chef’s knife we used in testing, and beet juice seeped into and stained the knife marks.

The Totally Bamboo Kauai bamboo board is totally fine. It looks nice enough, it’s lightweight, and it doesn’t stain as easily as other wood cutting boards. But the surface is harder than comparable boards, and in testing, it slid around quite a bit on the counter. It’s also a little high-maintenance for bamboo; you’re supposed to treat it with a food-grade mineral oil every few days for a month, then re-oil “as needed.”.

According to recent reports, the Angled Board from Material, which is generally available in FSC-certified walnut or carbon wood (the latter is actually stained white oak), would certainly make an attractive addition to a modern kitchen. But in testing we found that the smooth laminate coating highlights knife marks quite easily. It was also surprisingly slippery when we were cutting vegetables.

Farberware Nonslip Plastic Cutting Board.

Despite its name, the Farberware Nonslip Cutting Board didn’t stay put on the countertop during testing. On the other hand, though it’s not entirely stable, it is a nice size (14" x 10"), and the plastic construction makes it dishwasher-safe.

Nicole Home Flexible Plastic Cutting Board Mats.

Cutting boards (especially plastic ones) have one job, and that is to provide a protective layer between your knife and your counter. These flimsy “cutting board mats” didn’t, well, cut it in that department. They also slid around a lot when we were testing. If pressed, I’d say this type of cutting board (er, mat) could be handy to have around to put on top of a wood cutting board or butcher block countertop to help keep the wood clean and avoid cross-contamination when handling raw meat, but wouldn’t use this for chopping, slicing, or dicing directly on a stone countertop.

It has been revealed that the first thing you need to decide on when choosing a cutting board is which material you prefer. Here’s a rundown of what's good and bad about each.

PROS: Plastic cutting boards are useful as a supplement to a larger wooden board because they are lightweight and easy to carry around the kitchen. They are inexpensive, and they can go in the dishwasher. According to food director Chris Morocco, plastic is also a less absorbent material than wood (and about the same as rubber), which means they won’t harbor bacteria as easily. They’re a great choice for cutting raw meat.

It has been revealed that CONS: Plastic boards are harder on your knives than wooden or rubber boards. They will also get dinged up after heavy use, which makes them prone to trapping bacteria. Plastic boards will need to be replaced more often than their wooden counterparts. Some research demonstrates that microplastics in food could be linked to plastic cutting board use, but the research on the long-term health effects of microplastics remains unclear. You do run the risk of your cutting surface moving around a bit unless you go with one that’s designed to stay put like our top pick here. Chris recommends laying a damp dish towel, paper towel, or nonslip rubber mat under your plastic board to keep it steady. Again, we recommend using your plastic cutting boards supplementally, for less rigorous chopping tasks than your wooden chopping blocks.

WHO SHOULD BUY IT: If you’re the kind of home cook who is a dishwasher devotee, isn’t quite ready to invest in a cutting board, or wants to cut up raw chicken one day and mince garlic the next and needs a board that can be a totally clean slate each time, then plastic boards are the pick for you.

PROS: In general, wood is soft enough to protect your chef’s knife but still hard enough for smooth cuts, making it perfect for prepping everything except raw meat, Chris says. (Though you can do that, too, if you’re willing to give them a thorough soapy hand-washing afterward.) Another thing we love about wood boards is that they tend to “heal” themselves (i.e., they close up those knife marks after use), which prevents germ-harboring grooves from forming and keeps them in good shape for longer.

CONS: These boards require the most maintenance because wood is the most absorbent board material out there. They’re prone to retaining odors and stains, which means cleaning and caring for them is extra important—and requires more work than plastic or rubber. Scroll to the end for more on how to perform that care. We'll also note that an exception to the “easy on knives” rule is teak, which is a dense hardwood containing silica, a substance known to dull blades. So make sure to check which wood your board is made of, especially because teak boards tend to be less expensive.

WHO SHOULD BUY IT: Wood boards are best for those who care about beautiful objects and are game to give their kitchenware the care and attention it deserves—you know, the people who are regularly sharpening their knives, maintaining the seasoning on their cast-iron pans, and deep-cleaning their Dutch ovens.

End-grain wood vs. Edge-grain wood.

It has been revealed that wood cutting boards come in two styles: edge-grain and end-grain. In edge-grain cutting boards, the wood grains are aligned horizontally. In end-grain boards, the wood fibers are aligned vertically. End-grain boards are easier on your knives, because the knife blade slips between the fibers of the board rather than sliding across them. End-grain boards also self-heal better than edge-grain boards, because the fibers can come back together. End-grain boards dry more rapidly than edge-grain boards because the individual fibers are more exposed to air. This means they require more regular oiling. However, they are also far less likely to crack than edge-grain boards.

In previous versions of this review, we recommended edge-grain cutting boards because they tend to be less expensive. However, in our most recent upgrade we found plenty of end-grain boards that were within $20 to $30 dollars of their edge-grain competitors. Because the research really demonstrates that end-grain boards offer better longevity and are better for knife care, we’ve opted to recommend boards only in that style for our top picks this time around. Even if you invest in one that’s expensive (our favorite from Boardsmith), it will last you a very, very with proper care—the cost per use just makes sense.

Rubber cutting boards used to be found only in restaurant supply stores, but they have become more available on the market for regular home cooks in recent years—though they are still as expensive as wood boards.

Industry observers note that PROS: The rubber boards were some of our favorites in testing, because the material is so responsive. It’s lovely to slice on this springy surface. Rubber is soft, so it’s extremely easy on knives. The material is also non-porous, and therefore won’t absorb bacteria easily and is scratch resistant. They tend to have slightly textured surfaces, which is helpful for keeping them steady on the countertop. They’re super durable. While they aren’t usually dishwasher-safe, they don’t need any mineral oil applied (unlike wood cutting boards, which do); just wash them with mild detergent and leave them to air-dry.

Recent findings suggest that CONS: The only real cons here are that rubber cutting boards don’t have the luxe look and feel you get from a wood board. They also tend to be heavier and pricier than plastic ones.

There’s a reason these boards are so commonly found in sushi restaurants—the bouncy, softer surface supports a slicing motion rather than a rocking motion, making it optimal for ultra thin-bladed Japanese knives. If you like a heavier Western-style knife and use a rocking motion while chopping, this might not be the right board surface for you. Rubber boards are also quite heavy and difficult to maneuver around the kitchen, and they don’t look as nice as wooden boards.

WHO SHOULD BUY IT: Rubber cutting boards are great for people who like to use Japanese knives and want to invest in a piece of equipment that will last them for years to come, but doesn’t require a whole lot of upkeep.

Cutting board materials we don’t recommend.

How do you clean a plastic cutting board?

As mentioned above, plastic cutting boards are the most low-maintenance option, as you can simply pop (most of) them in the dishwasher. Though, if you’re cutting meat or fish, you need to scrape off any remnants under cold water before throwing it in. In restaurant kitchens, people often have a metal scraper that looks a bit like a palette knife for this; your stainless-steel bench scraper or plastic pastry scraper can also work. It prevents the proteins from cooking into the board’s nooks and crannies in hot water.

How do you clean a rubber cutting board?

Recent findings suggest that use that same cold water scraping technique if you have a rubber board, then follow with a hot, sudsy soap-up. Both rubber and plastic boards can be left to air-dry because they aren’t prone to warping.

How do you clean a wood cutting board?

In a recent development, wood cutting boards are a different story than any of the above materials. They’re high-maintenance–but also beautiful, long-lasting, and soft on your chef’s knife. Since you’re using your plastic or rubber board for raw meat (right?), a scrape-down followed by a warm, soapy hand-wash is usually enough for wood boards. Just don’t forget the underside. If you constantly get only one side of the board wet, you are unevenly hydrating the wood. Keep that same idea in mind when cutting: If your board is reversible, try to use both sides of it. If not, chop in different zones of your board to keep the surface evenly worn. That might sound like a lot, but if you chop in the same 2" quadrant daily, the angle on your board will swiftly change, which can cause slippage and, eventually, dull knives. Drying is the last, crucial step. With a clean dish towel, dry your board as thoroughly as possible. Then prop it up on its side until bone-dry to further guard against warping or cracking.

Because knife-friendly wood can harbor bacteria and is prone to staining, an occasional sanitizing session is necessary—and if you are using your wood board for meat, those sessions should be more frequent. Sprinkle any stained areas with coarse salt and rub them with the cut side of half a lemon. To disinfect, dilute some white vinegar with water and spray the surface of your board. Let it sit for a couple minutes before washing and drying. If necessary, you can also sanitize your wood board with a bleach solution, but be sure to dry and then oil it really well after.

In a recent development, POST-CLEANING CARE: Beyond washing, wood boards need to be treated with some TLC. Step right this way for an in-depth explainer on how to clean and care for it, but here’s the gist: At least once a month, pull out a clean microfiber cloth, a food-grade mineral oil, and a food-safe board sealant that combines oil with a protective beeswax. This is just as true if you have an inexpensive teak, acacia wood as it is if you go with something pricier, like a cherry or walnut cutting board.

Rub a small bit of the oil onto every surface of your dry, clean board. (You want the board to be really dry before you do this, so as to not seal in moisture.) Follow with the balm, which will buff into a creamy consistency. Don’t wipe that away just yet. Leave your board to deep-condition overnight, and then in the morning, gently wipe away any extra with a cloth or paper towel.

Microfiber Cleaning Cloths, Pack of 12.

Chicken Francese

📅 21 Jul 2021 | ⏱️ 3 min read (570 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Delish

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that chicken Francese is a staple at your favorite Italian restaurants.
  • It might seem strange, but it’s such an iconic flavor/texture combination.
  • According to recent reports, place 1 chicken breast on a cutting board.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that chicken Francese is a staple at your favorite Italian restaurants. But sometimes, you don't want to empty your wallet for this classic dinner favorite. That's where I come in! Francese is a preparation (much like Milanese) that can be used with all types of meat and seafood, from shrimp to veal. For chicken, it involves dredging cutlets in flour and beaten egg, creating a pseudo-batter. The cutlets are then pan-fried and made crispy, albeit temporarily. See, chicken Francese is one of those dishes that epitomizes "crispy gone soggy"—a texture sensation that is one of my absolute favorites. In this case, the chicken becomes "soggy" because you finish them by simmering it in a rich, lemony sauce that will knock your socks off.

It might seem strange, but it’s such an iconic flavor/texture combination. Also, it is very easy to make and comes together in under an hour. What could be better?!

According to recent reports, place 1 chicken breast on a cutting board. Using a sharp chef’s knife held parallel to the cutting board, slice into the thickest side of the breast, cutting three-quarters of the way through. Fold the top piece back (as if you were opening a book) and continue to cut until the breast is divided into 2 thinner cutlets. Repeat with the remaining chicken breast for a total of 4 cutlets. Working one piece at a time, place each cutlet between 2 sheets of plastic wrap. Using a meat mallet or the bottom of a small heavy skillet, pound the chicken to about 1/4" thick. Season all over with salt and pepper.

In a shallow dish, beat eggs, garlic powder, and a pinch of salt. Pour 1/2 cup flour into another shallow dish.

In a large, heavy skillet over medium heat, heat oil. Working in batches, coat cutlets in flour, shaking off excess, then dip into the egg mixture, turning to coat.

Place cutlets in the oil, being careful not to overcrowd the skillet, and cook, turning halfway through, until golden brown, 5 to 7 minutes.

Transfer cutlets to a paper towel-lined plate to drain and season with salt and pepper.

Wipe out the skillet, then heat over medium heat. Add five Tbsp. butter and the remaining one Tbsp. flour, stirring until just beginning to foam and the butter is melted, 3 to 5 minutes. Whisk in wine. Increase heat to medium-high and bring to a boil. Cook, stirring, until slightly reduced, 1 to 2 minutes. Add stock, lemon zest, and lemon juice and return to a boil. Reduce heat to medium and cook, whisking constantly, until the sauce is reduced by about one-third, 3 to 5 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add lemon slices and remaining 1 Tbsp. butter and cook, stirring, until the sauce is glossy, 2 to 3 minutes more.

Return chicken to the sauce and cook, turning halfway through, until heated through, 2 to 3 minutes.

Transfer chicken to a platter and pour the sauce over. Top with lemon slices and parsley.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Sources indicate that if you have any leftovers, store them in the refrigerator in an airtight container for up to 4 days. Luckily, this dish is used to being a tad soggy and lends itself well to being reheated in the microwave.

Meet the Stylists Who Shaped Vogue’s Best-Dressed List

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1623 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In case you missed it, Vogue’s 2026 best-dressed list has officially arrived—and on it are plenty of well-clad celebrities driving fashion forward.
  • According to recent reports, while all of these A-listers come with their own distinct sense of style, their masterful stylists have played an important role in making them true red-carpet stars.
  • Clients on Vogue’s best dressed list: Kendall Jenner, Carey Mulligan, Greta Lee, Ayo Edebiri.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In case you missed it, Vogue’s 2026 best-dressed list has officially arrived—and on it are plenty of well-clad celebrities driving fashion forward.

According to recent reports, while all of these A-listers come with their own distinct sense of style, their masterful stylists have played an important role in making them true red-carpet stars. As they say, “it takes a village”—so let’s pour one out for the amazing fashion minds who help craft all of the glamorous moments.

Clients on Vogue’s best dressed list: Kendall Jenner, Carey Mulligan, Greta Lee, Ayo Edebiri.

It has been revealed that styling approach: “My approach is always client-first. It’s key to me that what they wear on the red carpet feels authentic to who they are.”.

Favored silhouette: “I’m really drawn to silhouettes that feel a little unexpected and challenge convention, but still translate naturally to the red carpet.”.

Signature touch: “A quiet statement.”.

Most-pulled accessory: “A Sophie Buhai teardrop pouch.”.

Clients on Vogue’s best dressed list: Connor Storrie.

According to recent reports, styling approach: “I always start with the person rather than the clothes. For me, great styling is about understanding someone’s personality, proportions, and how they carry themselves, then building on that. With Connor, I’ve always drawn heavily on Old Hollywood, particularly the 1920s and 1930s, bringing those references into something that feels contemporary and a little unexpected. I want the clothes to enhance the person rather than overpower them. There’s nothing better than a beautifully executed look that feels completely effortless.”.

Favored silhouette: “I’m really drawn to a strong shoulder, a slightly higher waist, and a beautiful, long, wide-leg trouser. There’s something incredibly flattering and seductive about those proportions. I love the elegance of traditional menswear, but with a slightly louche, almost 1970s sensibility. It’s masculine without feeling rigid, and there’s a real sense of movement and ease to it.”.

Signature touch: “I think my strength is understanding proportion and knowing when to hold back. I’m much more interested in personal style than chasing trends. Sometimes the smallest adjustments to a jacket, the way a trouser falls or how a shirt sits against the body can completely transform a look. I also love finding that balance between classic elegance and a little sex appeal. Nothing should ever feel forced or as though someone’s wearing a costume.”.

Most-pulled accessory: “Pinky rings. I know they’re having a real moment on the red carpet, particularly in menswear, but they’re something I find myself coming back to. Even for Connor’s most recent red carpet at the Academy Museum Gala, convention might suggest wearing just one, but we loved both Tiffany & Co. rings so much that we decided to wear one on each pinky. One was a platinum ring featuring a cat’s-eye alexandrite surrounded by diamonds, while the other was a platinum ring set with a diamond of over eight carats. Two insanely beautiful pieces, and rather than choosing between them, we thought, why not wear both? I love those little moments where you go against the grain. Sometimes breaking an unwritten fashion rule creates something far more interesting and unexpected, and therein lies the fun of styling!”.

Clients on Vogue’s best dressed list: Teyana Taylor, Colman Domingo.

Recent findings suggest that styling approach: “Firstly, we consider the event and where our client is at that time in their career to decide what feels right for the moment. It’s also dependent on what our clients feel best in—making sure that they feel their truest and most confident self. Then, between the two of us, we also have to have synergy and feel good about a look, which we almost never disagree on.”.

Favored silhouette: “As we like to say—never waste a waist! We always love cinched-in jackets, corsets, and waistlines and are so happy to see them being modernized on both the runway and red carpet at the moment. Right now we are seeing waistlines highlighted through accentuated peplums, exaggerated hips, and snatched bodices.”.

It has been revealed that signature touch: “Jewelry is beyond crucial to us and always makes a look feel finished. Whether it’s diamonds, colored stones, or metal-based pieces, we love to use jewelry to elevate or put a twist on a look that might otherwise feel expected.”.

Most-pulled accessory: “We always gravitate towards a Christian Louboutin So Kate pump for our female clients, or the Christian Louboutin Ziggissimo heeled boot for our male clients.”.

Clients on Vogue’s best dressed list: Tessa Thompson, Whitney Peak.

Sources indicate that styling approach: “I think about the project, the event, and what we are communicating. But ultimately, I’m thinking about the woman I’m dressing, and what we have established as a fashion identity. And what makes them feel amazing.”.

It has been revealed that favored silhouette: “I’m not sure this defines my approach. When I see a look, it’s more that I connect it to a person. It’s much more organic and romantic than just saying, ‘Minis for spring!’”.

Signature touch: “My signature touch is that my clients look like they all have the best style, and that the clothes never wear them.”.

In a recent development, most-pulled accessory: “I love a mega earring. And a perfect little sack clutch. I just want to be Mrs. Prada!”.

Clients on Vogue’s best dressed list: Olivia Rodrigo.

According to recent reports, styling approach: “Our approach is rooted in the individuality of each client, creating looks that feel authentic yet unexpected. We love refined and timeless silhouettes but always need a little edge, or elements that aren’t so perfect. Ultimately, we want every look to tell a story, feel effortless, and leave an impression.”.

According to recent reports, favored silhouette: “We are really drawn to the two extremes right now—either something incredibly sculpted and structured, or fluid with beautiful draping. How a look moves, especially on the carpet, is so impactful.”.

Signature touch: “Our signature touch is finding the balance between femininity and edge—we love taking something traditionally beautiful and introducing an unexpected element via a shoe, accessory, fabric, or silhouette.”.

In a recent development, most-pulled accessory: “Our most pulled accessory is often a rare or untraditional shoe! We don’t always use them, but we are obsessed with interesting shoes.”.

Clients on Vogue’s best dressed list: Rebecca Hall, Morgan Spector.

Sources indicate that styling approach: “I always start with the person rather than the clothes. Understanding who they are, what makes them feel confident, and how they want to be perceived is essential. When putting together a look, I’m already considering the final image. The clothes, accessories, and glam all play a part, as does the way the client carries the look, how they pose, and how it’s photographed. The best looks are a creative collaboration between stylist, glam, and the client.”.

Favored silhouette: “Long column silhouette with a strong neckline.”.

Signature touch: “Clean lines with a touch of drama or tension.”.

Most-pulled accessory: “Black pointed toe pumps.”.

Clients on Vogue’s best dressed list: Daisy Edgar-Jones, Kendall Jenner.

Styling approach: “I always say I try to see my client’s style, just through my eyes. It always starts and ends with them, and that excitement when our visions align is when the relationship is magic.”.

Favored silhouette: “Knee-length skirts (even better if it’s a skirt suit), medium-sized bags, and square-toe heels—I can never get enough.”.

Signature touch: “Chic and cool. That combo is always what underwrites my vision. I’m always drawn to looks that say something but are still timeless—that make a moment in one part being really interesting, and the rest being really fluid, classic, or refined.”.

Most-pulled accessory: “Black satin slingback pumps and great sunglasses.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rockefeller IV, D-W.Va., questions witnesses during a Senate Finance hearing on health care on June 23, 2011.
  • Industry observers note that former Sen.
  • Rockefeller, who retired after the 2014 elections, played key roles on the tax-writing Senate Finance Committee, where he helped write landmark children’s health insurance legislation, as well as the Commerce, Science and Transportation and Intelligence panels which he chaired.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that sen. John D. Rockefeller IV, D-W.Va., questions witnesses during a Senate Finance hearing on health care on June 23, 2011. (Scott J. Ferrell/CQ Roll Call).

Industry observers note that former Sen. Jay Rockefeller, a five-term West Virginia Democrat and champion for the rural poor, has died at the age of 89.

Rockefeller, who retired after the 2014 elections, played key roles on the tax-writing Senate Finance Committee, where he helped write landmark children’s health insurance legislation, as well as the Commerce, Science and Transportation and Intelligence panels which he chaired.

A staunchly progressive lawmaker, he represented a deeply conservative state that turned further to the right in his later years. Rockefeller, scion of a famous Newly introduced York family renowned for its wealth, never wavered in his convictions and retired rather than face a potential backlash from voters upset by the then-Obama administration’s attempts to rein in the coal industry.

Recent findings suggest that sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., who challenged Rockefeller for his seat before he decided not to seek reelection, released a statement Friday praising her predecessor’s legacy.

“Jay dedicated his life to serving West Virginia and our nation, leaving a lasting legacy. He was always a true gentleman who treated me with respect, kindness, and encouragement,” Capito said. “Over the years, we developed a wonderful friendship that transcended politics, and I will always be grateful for that.”.

According to recent reports, west Virginia’s Republican Gov. Patrick Morrisey — himself a transplanted Northerner, with roots in Brooklyn and Latest Jersey — lauded Rockefeller’s record on health care and aid for coal miners and veterans in their adopted state.

“His work helped shape our state and left a lasting mark on the lives of generations of West Virginians,” Morrisey remarked.

In a recent development, rockefeller was born in Upcoming York City on June 18, 1937, the great-grandson of Standard Oil Co. founder John D. Rockefeller, who was once considered the world’s richest man. Rockefeller attended Harvard University, graduating with an A.B. in 1961. His passion was for the Far East and he spent three years studying at the International Christian University in Tokyo.

Sources indicate that he returned to the states and was appointed by President John F. Kennedy to the National Advisory Council of the Peace Corps in 1961, spearheaded the Peace Corps initial program in the Philippines. He worked for a brief time in what was then known as U.S. Department of Far Eastern Affairs before deciding to embark on a public service role of a more personal nature. He enrolling as a VISTA volunteer, in the program which would later be known as AmeriCorps, and moved to the small mining community of Emmons, W.Va., in 1964 at age 27.

Industry observers note that in West Virginia, Rockefeller found his life’s work. He described the experience as being “reborn,” and spoke often the poverty and hardship he encountered living in the small town. “I could not leave,” he stated of West Virginia. “I [had] become so devoted to those people and the unfairness.".

He had planned to remain only one year, but decided to stay and became active in local politics. He broke from his family's long tradition of Republican loyalty and ran successfully for the House of Delegates as a Democrat in 1966. Two years later, he was elected secretary of state.

According to recent reports, rockefeller lost a bid for governor in 1972, but he became the president of West Virginia Wesleyan College and continued to place roots in the state. He married Sharon Percy Rockefeller in 1967 and they started their family. When he ran for governor again in 1976, he won, and served two terms before winning election to the U.S. Senate in 1984, ultimately serving five terms before retiring in 2014.

According to recent reports, rockefeller was determined to increase economic opportunities for West Virginia, for whom he felt was forgotten and abandoned by the rest of the country. He called the people of his state “the hardest-working people I know,” and believed that bringing more business opportunities would help lift the state out of severe rural poverty and the dependence on the coal industry.

Rockefeller traveled to Japan and worked tirelessly to bring a Toyota manufacturing plant to Buffalo, W.Va, one of over twenty Japanese companies he’d brought to West Virginia. He fought for fair trade policies and targeted tax relief to protect West Virginia industries such as steel and chemicals.

Coal mining had long been the economic backbone of West Virginia, but Rockefeller felt more must be done to protect miners, many of whom worked in unsafe conditions or fell ill with pneumoconiosis, or black lung disease, after years of inhaling coal dust.

But defying the coal industry came with a political cost. When Rockefeller originally ran for governor in 1972, he had opposed mountaintop mining, also called strip mining, or the practice of removing large amounts of earth and rock in order to access underground seams of coal. When he ran again in 1976, he reversed his position and won.

But even as he ascended to the Senate, Rockefeller remained both friend and foe to the coal industry.

Industry observers note that despite growing up on the Upper East Side of Manhattan, figuratively and literally hundreds of miles away from coal mines, Rockefeller understood its deep roots in West Virginia’s economy and culture. He believed it was the miners — rather than industry — for whom he was defending.

He hung a century-old photo of a coal miner in his Senate office in the Hart building, and would point to the photo and remark to visitors that “this is why I’m here and who I work for.”.

Rockefeller fought to secure pensions for miners, especially as coal companies would file for bankruptcy and immediately restructure to do away with pension plans.

In 1990, Rockefeller was one of only 11 senators to vote against the bipartisan Clean Air Act, which he felt disadvantaged workers in West Virginia. But those close to him mentioned the decision weighed heavily on him, and Rockefeller privately worried that the lack of such regulations would pollute the air and destroy waterways, the brunt of which would be born by the same disadvantaged people whom he vowed to protect.

In a recent development, he believed strongly in the deliberative aspects of the legislative process, consuming great amounts of reading material to familiarize himself with the complications. During a time of increasing partisan rancor, Rockefeller still reached across the aisle to find a willing partner, even when there was not one to be found.

In 2010, as the Environmental Protection Agency’s greenhouse gas regulations were coming to fruition, Rockefeller came up with a compromise to delay implementation for two years.

He viewed himself as a broker between industry interests and the hard working people from coal-states like West Virginia. He had hoped that his years of standing up for coal miners and West Virginia interests would foster enough goodwill among industries primed to oppose any compromise that was less than an all-out rejection of the existing EPA statutes.

It has been revealed that but industry walked away from Rockefeller, preferring a hard-line opposition to EPA regulations, and lobbied other senators to vote against Rockefeller’s measure. Furious, Rockefeller took to the floor of the Senate to denounce the coal industry and its leaders, an unprecedented action for a popular coal-state senator.

Recent findings suggest that “The reality is that many who run the coal industry today would rather attack false enemies and deny real problems then find solutions,” he said on the Senate floor in June 2012. “Scare tactics are a cynical waste of time, money and, worst of all, coal miners’ hopes. But sadly, these coal operators have closed themselves off from any other opposing voices and few dared to speak out for change — even though it’s been staring them in the face for years.”.

His fury against the coal industry was heard loudly, many speculating that he would retire rather than face reelection.

Recent findings suggest that he had won reelection to the Senate handily during his five campaigns. In 2008, his final election, he was reelected with nearly 64 percent of the vote. But six months following his fated coal speech, in January 2013, Rockefeller announced he would retire at the end of his fifth term.

It has been revealed that rockefeller’s legacy may best be known for his fight to expand health care for vulnerable populations, including children, the economically disadvantaged and the elderly. Rockefeller served as one of the chief congressional champions for President Bill Clinton’s proposed health care overhaul, and later he played a critical role and was a loud progressive voice in writing and passing the Affordable Care Act in the Senate.

Sources indicate that rockefeller believed strongly in a public health insurance option, offering it as an amendment in the Senate Finance Committee during the ACA markup. A public-run insurance blueprint, he said, would put patients before profits, and help those people, especially West Virginians, with high health care costs and poor coverage who were left “out in the cold.”.

Industry observers note that "These are people," Rockefeller stated, visibly emotional during his closing arguments to the Senate Finance Committee. "Eleven-year-old kids. These are families, and we have to respect them. And you respect them by giving them a choice.".

Recent findings suggest that the amendment was rejected. Rockefeller pivoted to strengthening Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Program provisions, believing that poor and disadvantaged families could seek refuge within those programs. CHIP had been one of Rockefeller’s signature legislative victories, helping to write that program initially in 1997 and later working on a major expansion that became law in 2009.

Despite his initial concerns and later disappointments — at one time saying publicly he could not support the measure as it stood — he later added his support to the ACA, citing it as a win for all Americans and actively lobbied his colleagues to support it.

According to recent reports, rockefeller was also known for his role on the Senate Intelligence Committee. A former chairman, he was critical of the nation's mismanagement of the Iraq war and clashed frequently with Republicans over the treatment of detainees. After he retired from Congress, Rockefeller served as a distinguished fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations.

Industry observers note that respect for Rockefeller ran deep on Capitol Hill. He was beloved by staff and known as a thoughtful, deliberative lawmaker. He had a fondness for classical music and served as a board member of the Bach Consort, an organization in Washington devoted to the study and performance of the music of Bach and his contemporaries. He admired art and Asian culture, and served as a board member of the Asia Society.

In a recent development, rockefeller is survived by his wife, Sharon Percy Rockefeller; four children: John D. Rockefeller V, Valerie Rockefeller, Charles Rockefeller and Justin Rockefeller; and nine grandchildren.

Disclosure: the author served as a staffer in Rockefeller’s Senate office from 2009-11.

It has been revealed that there are only so many dishes you can make in your oven on Thanksgiving, so we’ve made it easy for you with a no-bake stuffing that doesn’t require taking up oven space. Instead, we use a slow cooker that’ll help you whip up your stuffing alongside the stars of the show (roast turkey and pumpkin pie, obviously!). While you buzz around the kitchen, the slow cooker will cook your stuffing for you — resulting in a delicious Thanksgiving side dish waiting for you to serve up.

Arrange a rack in the center of the oven and preheat it to 350°. Spread bread on a baking sheet. Bake the bread, tossing it halfway through, until it is crispy and feels dry. The edges should just be starting to turn golden, which should take about 15 to 20 minutes. Meanwhile, melt butter in a large skillet over medium heat. When melted, add celery, onion, and herbs. Season with salt and pepper and cook until the onions are translucent, about 7 minutes. Remove from heat and let cool.

Sources indicate that grease your Crock-Pot bowl and add the toasted bread. Pour the vegetable mixture, eggs, broth, and parsley over the bread. Toss to combine and cover.

Recent findings suggest that cook on low for 3 to 4 hours, stirring after 2 hours have passed. Garnish with parsley before serving.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Thanksgiving is hectic; we get it. This is the perfect dish to set aside while you prepare everything else. After the 3-hour cook time, switch the pot to the "keep warm" setting—just give it a stir every 30 minutes or so to make sure the bread around the edges doesn't dry out. If the stuffing is ready hours before dinner time, you can add up to ¼ cup of broth every few hours to keep things hydrated.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that it is fun to be contrarian. I admit to the light thrill it gives me to tell people that I hate oat milk, or that I prefer a wet martini. It’s healthy for all of us to have our preferences. But sometimes what should be a matter of personal taste goes viral, amassing an army of haters who make this preference their entire personality. Think back to the great cake vs. pie wars of the 2010s, when anyone who admitted to liking cake was a tasteless rube. This isn’t even about what you like anymore—it’s about the attention that comes with going against the mainstream.

This is all to say that complaining about turkey on Thanksgiving has got to stop. It is good, and I need people to stop pretending as if it’s not.

Sources indicate that you would think from the way people talk about turkey around Thanksgiving that a flock of the birds came into their house and killed their mother. In 2020, Business Insider wrote that turkey isn’t good and you should leave it off your Thanksgiving table. Vox insists the (horrifying) numbers of turkeys wasted every year are in service of “a dry, flavorless bird no one likes,” while Milk Street claims anyone who likes it must be “pretending.” Even this very publication called it “The Big Freaky Chicken.”.

In a recent development, respectfully, what on earth are you people talking about? Every year I cannot wait for the unveiling of the turkey. It is the ultimate reminder that this isn’t a normal meal because we do not eat turkey on the regular.

Over the years, my family has more often entrusted me with the cooking. We tend to do a version of this Martha Stewart en papillote method and I relish in the work. There is care required to ensure the meat is juicy and golden, and the resulting gravy silky and rich. There is great satisfaction in carrying out the gorgeous centerpiece. There is a subtle butteriness to the meat, and something wilder that even the most factory farmed bird can’t erase. Roasting a chicken is for a Tuesday. Roasting a turkey is for when you have the day off work.

Part of the joy of the turkey, of course, is the leftovers. Turkey congee, turkey pot pie, turkey melts, which will only exist because of Thanksgiving. A feast stretched out, reminding you that abundance does not last for just a day. Do not rob yourself of such plenty.

Obviously, the haters have not stopped millions of turkeys from being served every Thanksgiving. The biggest complaint seems to be that the turkey is never cooked well. And I’ll give you that, with a bigger bird, that you only encounter once a year, it takes planning and effort to ensure the middle doesn’t become a powdery mess while the legs are still raw. But I don’t know, try. There are many things that are tricky to cook that are beloved precisely because of the exhilaration of the challenge, so I don’t know why turkey gets all the heat.

If you’re here, it means you like to cook, even love it, and there are no shortage of recipes guiding you toward bird nirvana. So put your hobby to good use, get a meat thermometer, and figure it out. Because as much fun as it is to be a hater, it’s even more fun to prove everyone wrong with a feast.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If—for a certain set of cool, young designers—doing bridal was once thought uncool, 2026 may have been the year that finally put that notion to rest.

Sources indicate that we’ve been seeing the shift for years now: For many brides, the wedding-day dream has gone beyond the beautiful, white, traditionally “bridal” wedding dress. Increasingly, brides want something, well, cool—an expression of their personal brand and sensibility, whether that means a painstakingly sourced archival look or a custom piece by an unexpected designer. This year, that trend was on full display, as wedding fashion increasingly became a stage and cultural touchpoint for brides and designers alike.

2026 was a banner year for high-profile weddings and celebrity brides wearing everything from romantic gowns to razor-sharp suits: Zendaya and Tom Holland, Dua Lipa and Callum Turner, Dove Cameron and Damiano David, Cristiano Ronaldo and Georgina Rodríguez, Emma Roberts and Cody John, Karl-Anthony Towns and Jordyn Woods, to name just a few.

Industry observers note that and that’s without even mentioning the “royal wedding” of Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce. While the photos are yet to be released (and if you ask Swift bestie Dakota Johnson, they never will be), we do know that Swift became Jonathan Anderson’s first celebrity bride, a move that had people feverishly searching for clues at his Dior Haute Couture show in July. Could it be that white chiffon and degradé lace final gown, which later graced the runway at Vogue World: Milan? Nothing was revealed, apart from Anderson telling Women’s Wear Daily, “It was a joy to work with her. We became very good friends,” and “It’s an emotional thing doing someone’s wedding.”.

Dua Lipa’s August wedding, meanwhile, was a fashion extravaganza, starting with a custom Schiaparelli white skirt suit, designed by creative director Daniel Roseberry. Who can forget the image of the pop star, beaming under a burst of confetti as she walked out of the town hall as a newlywed? Her suit was inspired by Bianca Jagger’s bridal look for her wedding to Mick Jagger in Saint-Tropez on May 12, 1971, perhaps the ultimate cool-girl bridal nod. Lipa rounded out her bridal looks with a white leather Bottega Veneta custom gown by Louise Trotter, and a Chanel haute couture gown for her main wedding dress.

Dua Lipa in Chanel haute couture.

According to recent reports, beyond the celeb wedding world, this year saw rising stars and in-demand designers put forward bridal looks, some for the first time. Dilara Findikoglu debuted her first bridal capsule, a rule-breaking, lingerie-forward offering adapted from her ready-to-wear line, with campaign photos of models smashing plates, smoking, and mounting their grooms. (“I really believe that the power of my clothes is to bring out the uniqueness in someone,” Findikoglu previously told Vogue. “That’s exactly why they became Dilara Brides: to reveal the most unique version of who they already are.”).

Dilara Findikoglu’s debut bridal collection.

Sources indicate that batsheva debuted her first bridal collection at Newly introduced York’s Bridal Fashion Week. Christopher John Rogers solidified his status as a sought-after designer for stylish brides, including Vogue fashion market director Naomi Elizée Blue, TikTok brand strategist Ali Lebow, and film director Pam Nasr. In an interview with The New York Times about his rising profile in the wedding world, Rogers even teased his very own bridal collection.

Naomi Elizée Blue in Christopher John Rogers.

CFDA/Vogue Fashion Funders Zoe Gustavia Anna Whalen and Miss Claire Sullivan created custom bridal looks for Architectural Digest senior design editor Hannah Martin and the artist Tourmaline, respectively. Martin’s gown was inspired by a look from Whalen’s spring 2025 collection, featuring a corseted bodice with a padded hip. Whalen previously told Vogue about why she decided to take on a bridal client, a rare move for her. “It aligns so much with my general ethos of garments being these weighted, emotional objects,” Whalen mentioned. “So when it’s the right fit, being able to create that with such intention for somebody else is so beautiful.”.

Tourmaline (right) in Miss Claire Sullivan.

According to recent reports, elsewhere, Raul Lopez dressed his friends Juice Rodriguez and Cristal Veras in coordinated Luar for their Fresh York wedding. Gabbriette became the first bride for Matières Fécales, the cult Paris label whose show Rihanna attended in September. And Colleen Allen, winner of the 2026 CFDA Emerging Designer of the Year Award, has quietly become the fashion girls’ dream wedding dress designer, after making a custom look for Charli xcx’s wedding reception last year.

According to recent reports, “Bridal” no longer means just one thing. For independent designers, it can be a playground to express something newly introduced, a platform for their brand, and, as Joe Bobowicz observed in a Vogue Business article, a dependable revenue stream. And as people expand their ideas of what a wedding can look like—donning colorful gowns in every color from butter yellow to pink to black, and playing with material and silhouette—as we head into 2027, the future of bridal style has never been more thrillingly uncertain.

#100863. Industry News: I Prepared for This A.I. Chaos Moment for Over a Year. Here Is What I’ve Learned.
